item.title: Democrats see a path to Congress as electoral worries spread into Trump country
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democrats' wary optimism about the midterms gave way to growing confidence this week. The party has seen strong post-Labor Day polls in key battlegrounds - and even in traditionally red areas. Recent escalations in the war in Iran, including an attack on a major pipeline in Saudi Arabia, mean the rising gas prices bedeviling Republicans will not be going down anytime soon. Republicans have not been able to bring prices under control more generally. And President Donald Trump's unpopularity is at near-record levels. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Considering all this, Democrats now think conditions are right for the party to retake control of the House and possibly the Senate later this year. "If the election were held today, we would win the majority," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (New York) said in an interview with The Washington Post. Schumer said he felt "considerably more bullish" about Democrats' chances of retaking the Senate than he did a few months ago. He described the environment as uncannily similar to 2006, when discontent with the war in Iraq helped Democrats recapture the Senate and the House. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Massachusetts) said Democrats' recent momentum is driven by their focus on the economy, with voters believing that the party understands the financial pain they've felt in the years since Republicans swept into unified control. "That is what is driving these polls," Clark told The Post on Thursday. Still, Democratic fears remain. Democrats need at least four more seats to take the Senate majority and would have to win at least two in states Trump carried by double-digit margins in 2024. Republicans are seeking to blunt any Democratic gains by flipping Democratic-held open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire, where polls show competitive races. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the Senate contest in New Hampshire from "Lean Democrat" to "Toss Up" this week. Republicans focused on keeping control of the House argue that they have a more favorable map, partly because a GOP redistricting effort has limited the number of battleground districts, and partly because they believe that Democratic primary voters nominated weak candidates in a handful of key races. Then there is the incoming flood of GOP money. Republicans are set to spend nearly $140 million more on ads than Democrats are in the nine most competitive races in the final weeks of the campaign, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The disparity is especially yawning in the Senate contest in Texas, where Republicans have reserved $39.6 million in ads and Democrats have reserved just $5.1 million. On the House side, the National Republican Congressional Committee plans to run coordinated ads in 39 districts, with more than $24 million in ads reserved. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has plans for coordinated ads in 14 districts. "The Republican campaign engines are firing on all cylinders, and we are burying House Democrats in battleground districts across the country," said Mike Marinella, spokesperson for House Republicans' campaign arm. "Republicans have the historic fundraising advantage, a more favorable map, stronger candidates, and the firepower to defy history and grow our House majority." Schumer acknowledged Republicans' financial advantage but said it would not stop Democrats from retaking the Senate. "We don't need as much money as them given the political climate, given the terrain," he said. "All we need is enough to stay in the ballpark and be able to answer them." Republicans have begun to openly acknowledge electoral concerns in recent weeks, particularly with polls showing that Democrats are far more eager to vote than Republicans are. Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told reporters Thursday that he was going to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa to raise money for GOP Senate candidates. "If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn't have believed you. Those ought to be fat guy layups for us," he said, though he predicted Republicans would hold those seats. "The far left, they're angry," Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said this week on the "Pod Force One" podcast, describing this as a "challenging environment" for his party. "They hate President Trump with a burning passion. And they're going to crawl over broken glass to vote." Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) acknowledged Wednesday that Republicans are facing "headwinds" but said the Senate races that will decide control of the chamber remain competitive. "It's not a great environment for us," Thune said. "But we've got really quality candidates in all the competitive races, and the polling that we're seeing in those races shows that these races are tight." Republicans have been debating how to increase enthusiasm beyond spending more money. Some, largely those closely tied to the president and his political operation, argue that the path to victory is to re-create the electorate Trump built in 2024. Other Republicans - primarily those in battleground districts where private and public polls show that voters are deeply upset with the president - believe the way to win is to distance themselves from the administration and its policies, a difficult task following a decade of Trump remaking the party in his own image. "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump said during one of two speeches he gave at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas recently. "Just one more time." Trump has made it difficult for many candidates, especially those in tight races, to embrace this tactic. In large part, that's because he has repeatedly dismissed the issue that voters say is their main stressor: prices. His trade war has raised prices on goods across the country. And gas prices, which have shot up because of the president's war against Iran, are nearing $4.50 per gallon on average. However, speaking at a campaign rally Wednesday in North Carolina, a state he has won in three straight presidential elections, Trump said high fuel prices were "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we have done" in Iran. A Republican operative working on House races, speaking on the condition of anonymity to be candid, responded to Trump's comments with an animated image of actor Bryan Cranston screaming, "F---!" The president has promised to get out the vote for Republican candidates, including those in trouble deep in Trump country. Some have taken him up on his offer, but not every candidate wants him around, and administration officials' visits to red states have been seen as warning signs for Republicans. Vice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas this week to stump for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tighter-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Trump and Vance won Kansas by 16 percentage points in 2024. Vance is also set to campaign in Iowa on Friday. But the state's Republican Senate nominee, Rep. Ashley Hinson, will not appear next to the vice president. A Hinson spokesperson cited previously scheduled events, but the absence comes as the candidate seeks to tout her bipartisan record in a state Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024. Hinson is locked in a tight race against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. And in South Florida, an area Trump dominated in 2024, Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar openly broke with the president Thursday. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says directly to the camera in a new campaign ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Democrats say they began to see a change during what was supposed to be Republicans' hallmark 2026 event: the party's unorthodox midterm convention. The gathering was billed as a way for the GOP to showcase its front-line candidates, but instead it featured Trump defending his record and pledging to give each American adult a $5,000 check if Republicans hold Congress this year, a proposal many Democrats saw as a sign of desperation. "We're not measuring the drapes, but the ground has shifted," said Xochitl Hinojosa, a longtime Democratic operative and top spokesperson at the Democratic National Committee after the 2016 election. Some Democratic operatives running campaigns said they had been waiting to see whether Republicans would coalesce around a clear affordability message during the Texas event. But when it became obvious that the event would be a Trump-centric celebration that offered no direct case for why Republicans deserved unified control for two more years, their confidence grew. "Turns out breaking all your campaign promises and doing everything possible to make life more expensive for everyone is bad politics," said Viet Shelton, spokesperson for House Democrats' campaign arm. "Shocker." The last time Democrats experienced a wave election was in 2018, when the party swept into control of the House two years after Trump's first presidential win. Meredith Kelly, a Democratic operative who was the top spokesperson at House Democrats' campaign arm at the time, said that there are plenty of similarities between that year and this one - primarily around Trump's unpopularity - but that the biggest difference is how Republicans' worries are coming from voters who helped them win in 2024, such as rural voters and Black and Latino men. "Their coalition's floor is falling out from underneath them," said Kelly. The prospect of a wave election has Democratic candidates in districts once thought entirely unreachable for the party feeling like they may have a shot to do the unexpected in November. Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy veteran running against GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert in a district that spans eastern Colorado, knows that her odds of winning have always been long. Trump won the district less than two years ago by 18 percentage points. But powered almost entirely by anger at Washington and voters' fears about their personal finances, Laubacher thinks she has an opportunity to take down her outspoken Republican opponent. "People vote frequently about their pocketbooks and their wallets, but I think the situation is growing ever more fraught for people," said Laubacher. "Every aspect of their life has become more expensive, and they do not feel that the government is doing anything about any of it." Jarrell Dillard contributed to this report. item.title: Google says Gemini hacked real systems after mistaking them for a test
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Google said it did not consider the unauthorized logins to rise to the level of misalignment, the AI industry term for software going rogue or not following instructions. (David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images file) Google on Friday disclosed the first known instance of its artificial intelligence software, Gemini, carrying out an undirected computer hack, weeks after similar disclosures by AI firms Anthropic and OpenAI raised security alarms about AI models going beyond the instructions of their human creators. Google said in a statement that in May its AI model gained unauthorized access to three outside systems during a test by either guessing login information or using login credentials it found in a public repository. Heather Adkins, a Google vice president for security engineering, said in the statement that the AI model thought that the outside computer systems “were part of the test,” but she said in all three instances, the model stopped before doing anything further with its access. “In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” she said. Google said it did not consider the unauthorized logins to rise to the level of misalignment, the AI industry term for software going rogue or not following instructions. Instead, the company said the intrusions resulted from mistaken identity, where Gemini thought it was operating within a test but was actually connected to the real internet. Google said the model corrected itself and the company believed the intrusions did not cause any damage. “These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins said. Fears about AI agents going rogue have spiked in recent months since OpenAI said in July that one of its agents had hacked an AI startup , Hugging Face. OpenAI has continued to disclose what it calls examples of other “ unexpected or concerning ” behavior by AI agents, and Anthropic has described similar behavior by its AI software, Claude. The OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco. Fears about AI agents going rogue have spiked in recent months. (David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images) Sydney Von Arx, CEO of Nightingale Collective, an organization focused on AI safety, questioned why Google did not disclose the intrusions sooner. “At this point I think it’s clear we cannot expect companies to voluntarily come forward and publicly disclose when their agents go rogue, escape, and hack companies,” she said. She also said she believed Google was too hasty to say that the incidents don’t rise to the level of misalignment. “That’s exactly what Anthropic said after their incidents,” she said. Anthropic later said its “preliminary analysis was constrained due to our desire to disclose incidents in a timely manner.” Google said the company did not learn about the intrusions until July, when Irregular, an AI-focused cybersecurity company that was carrying out the tests on Gemini when the intrusions occurred, reviewed its work to look for incidents similar to the Hugging Face disclosure. Google said it then investigated, informed the organizations behind the websites of the intrusions and told federal authorities about the hacks. Irregular said it did not believe the incident to be a “sophisticated cyber action” and “there are no current open issues.” It said it planned to release a paper in a few weeks “to share best practices for containment and securely running cyber evals.” The intrusions were reported earlier Friday by The Wall Street Journal . AI safety concerns have now reached a fever pitch , with a handful of AI researchers resigning from their jobs and a diverse array of people calling for coordinated action to protect the security of vital systems. Those calls, though, have met with skepticism from the White House and in the Chinese government. item.title: U.S. military had close call after using AI to generate intelligence report
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Army soldiers conduct unmanned aerial system training in April 2026. - Spc. Alva Gonzalez/US Army The intelligence report, circulated across the US military this spring in the midst of the war with Iran, immediately set off alarm bells: A Chinese ship in the Middle East was transporting components of a nuclear weapons program. The US military swung into action with plans to intercept the vessel, according to four sources familiar with the episode. According to two of the sources, armed members of the US military were preparing to board the ship. Military planes were in the air, one of those sources and another source familiar with the incident said. It was only just before the planned operation that officials dug deeper into the report put together by a special operations command analyst and found it had been generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) — and that a chatbot the analyst had used inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying. CNN was not able to learn what the misidentified cargo was. The report, according to one of the sources, was “entirely false.” But it also “almost started a war,” the source said. Any US operation against a Chinese vessel could have risked spiraling into an armed conflict between the two nations. Across the US military and the intelligence community, officials are pushing to weave AI into nearly every facet of their work, from analyzing the huge volumes of raw intelligence the US collects and selecting targets for strikes, to more mundane applications like managing budgeting, logistics and supply chains. But the episode underscores the profound risks of using this powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology for targeting in the middle of a war. Analysts have long feared that AI could lead to a catastrophic miscalculation if nation states are relying on poor or corrupted data — the kind of miscalculation that might lead the United States to fire on a Chinese ship based on inaccurate information. In this particular instance, the analyst queried a chatbot about some intelligence reporting on the ship’s manifest that originated with US Special Operations Command Pacific, based in Hawaii. It was not clear whether the chatbot was a commercially available one or a US government product. “The internal tools are mostly just copies of the commercial stuff wearing lipstick,” a former senior US official familiar with the AI systems used by military and intelligence analysts. The bot fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings and reached its fateful conclusion about the material the ship was carrying. The analyst then used AI again to package the findings into a standard intelligence report — the kind that is trusted by military officials — and disseminated it. US Special Operations Command Pacific and the Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. The rationale for the rapid adoption of AI is that it can help the military make battlefield decisions, like which targets to strike or which military assets to move where, faster. Officials say the US can’t afford to fall behind in integrating AI in case it must one day fight China or another adversary who would potentially be able to stay one step ahead of the US. In January, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released his agency’s “Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy” in a bid to speed up the military’s use of AI. “We will unleash experimentation, eliminate bureaucratic barriers, focus our investments and demonstrate the execution approach needed to ensure we lead in military AI,” Hegseth said in a speech announcing the strategy . Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, DC. - Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images The strategy also pushes for its broad use across the military, ordering the department to make AI available via several programs with the aim of “democratizing AI experimentation and transformation across the Department by putting America’s world-leading AI models directly in the hands of our three million civilian and military personnel, at all classification levels,” a memo announcing the strategy said . But the effort is decentralized, multiple US officials familiar with the dynamic said, with different parts of the government using different tools under different orders and safety standards. There’s no one set of standards for how the US verifies the information generated by these tools. The constellation of different AI systems being deployed by disparate corners of the military and intelligence community means that the relative reliability and functionality vary widely. For weeks, Washington policymakers have been intensely debating AI after a series of dire warnings from Silicon Valley engineers and tech CEOs of the possibility that AI could break free of human constraints, with potentially civilization-ending consequences. But the episode with the Chinese ship underscores a different, and more immediate risk: human beings making disastrous decisions based on inaccurate or misleading information generated by AI or other automated systems. Sources said that the military is rapidly turning to AI to help with targeting, an area which holds the obvious risk of fatal mistakes. “AI in targeting is definitely something that is ramping up and there is no real guidance for how having a human in the loop will prevent civilian casualties or fratricide,” another source familiar with the military’s current policies said. The kind of “ hallucination ” that the tool used by the analyst in this case conjured has not been an isolated incident across the intelligence community since these tools began proliferating across government, according to one of the sources. For some older intelligence officials — even those who broadly support the use of AI inside the military — AI has put pressure on analysts to produce and disseminate intelligence faster, opening the door for mistakes. Young analysts in particular, several sources said, are natives on these tools and more likely to trust them uncritically. “AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster,” one of the sources said. item.title: California homes are falling into the sea. The fight to save them is getting ugly.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Caroline Brehman/For The Washington Post) DANA POINT, California – Natalie Driessen drove down Beach Road on a mission, past neighbors whose houses fell into the sea and others now scrambling to prevent their property from collapsing next. She had a video from March that she wanted everyone to see. When she spotted an Orange County supervisor outside what was left of one mangled kitchen and living room, Driessen pulled out her phone to play the clip of the California Coastal Commission — the powerful state agency tasked with preserving beaches — discussing a home in her gated community. California beaches are considered public beyond a certain high tide line, the commissioners warned, and that waterline was rising. “I wonder,” one of the commissioners said , “how many years before I’m allowed to just pull up a chair — sit in their, you know, front deck porch and watch TV because it’s public land. … I don’t think we’re that far away from this, right?” Get The 7 newsletter The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free Storms and high tides — fueled by a near record-breaking El Niño — have battered the California coast in recent weeks, destroying homes and eroding beaches. The fallout has supercharged years-long tensions between the owners of coveted oceanfront property and the authorities they say aren’t doing enough to protect them. Natalie Driessen in front of her Dana Point home. It is still standing, but her backyard was wrecked. - (Caroline Brehman/For The Washington Post) The damage has intensified a bigger debate playing out around the coast: What can or should be done to save private property in the most vulnerable communities? Driessen was furious about the March clip — convinced the authorities wanted her and other beachfront homeowners to give up and leave in the face of sea damage. “We’re paying taxes!” the 51-year-old plastic surgeon told the county supervisor indignantly. On Beach Road in Dana Point — which has been home and second-home to actors, famous athletes and members of the Disney family — the destruction has residents fuming and banding together. They’re organizing in a group chat and paying more than $50,000 per household, they say, to build a rock wall along the shore, desperate and rushing to stave off further damage with another El Niño-driven surge expected in a couple weeks. Residents want to make the rock wall permanent, but “coastal armoring” is so controversial that the California Coastal Commission generally bans it in new developments. “It’s important to note that while seawalls can provide temporary relief for homes, they can also increase erosion and destroy the public beaches that help protect those same structures,” Joshua Smith, a spokesperson for the Coastal Commission, said in a statement. Smith said the commission has “for years repeatedly engaged the community and the city on medium- to longer-term strategies for preventing flood damage in this area,” adding that the agency has suggested installing a cobblestone berm, elevating homes or adding sand to beaches. The commission approved emergency permits for the Beach Road rock barrier, which it says will cover 17 properties. But many residents are refusing to sign the papers — outraged that they may have to tear the wall down after 120 days if they do not get permanent approval. Everyone agrees the community, and others like it, need a long-term plan to deal with the eroding beach. But they disagree over what that should look like, and who is to blame for the erupting crisis. “When we have these emergencies like what happened last week, the responses are ad hoc ... and generally they may not lead to better, good long term outcomes,” said Charles Lester, a former Coastal Commission director who now directs an ocean policy center at UC Santa Barbara. “Once the rock goes on the beach it’s very hard to bring it back up.” One long-term option for vulnerable communities, Lester said, may be retreat. “At what point do we start to recognize that maybe it’s not a good idea to have the development there?” Lester said. “If we get to that point, the question is not, ‘Okay, leave,’ it’s more like — ‘Okay, how do we facilitate a community transition?’” Replacing the beach sand is another possible solution — but those efforts are expensive and could take years. “If California is good at anything in this world, it’s bureaucracy,” Dana Point Mayor John Gabbard lamented in an interview. The residents of Beach Road know that not everyone sympathizes with wealthy families losing their second homes with ocean views. Driessen sees comments on social media that suggest they deserve the misfortune. Some say they should have seen it coming in the risky business of beachfront real estate. Driessen says she worked hard for her dream beach house, purchased two years ago. She took out loans and put herself through school. Now her backyard is destroyed; her home is still standing but at risk whenever the next storm hits. item.title: Is Trump's latest White House media ban legal? Recent history shows mixed signals.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – If recent history is the judge, President Donald Trump faces an uncertain legal landscape after his latest attempt to ban certain media outlets from covering him at the White House . Trump announced in a Sept. 18 social media post that he is banning reporters from three major media outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and Politico – from the White House because he views their coverage as "FAKE NEWS." Trump later said there wasn't a specific incident or story that prompted him to initiate the ban, which would not preclue the outlets from reporting on the president. "It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," he said. It's not the first time the Trump administration has taken such action against the press. During his first term, the Trump White House in 2018 pulled the press credentials of CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, complaining that he refused to yield the microphone at a press conference. However, a federal judge appointed by Trump later forced the White House to restore the press pass, saying Acosta hadn't been given a proper chance to defend himself. And in early 2025, the White House blocked the Associated Press from the Oval Office, The White House East Room, and the press pool that sometimes travels with the president. The White House was upset because the AP declined to change its style for describing the gulf bordering the U.S. and Mexico from the "Gulf of Mexico" to the "Gulf of America." Trump had ordered the name change on official maps . In the AP's case, one federal trial judge appointed by Trump temporarily blocked the ban. But two appeals court judges - also appointed by Trump - on the three-judge panel reversed that decision in a 2-1 ruling. The case is still being litigated. The past controversial decisions make for an uncertain legal landscape if the latest media outlets decide to take the White House to court for the most recent ban. A spokesperson for CNN told USA TODAY in a statement that the ban Trump proposes would be an "illegal assault" on the press. The network said it plans to continue its coverage. "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting," the statement said. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government." Politico, in a statement, said the publication "will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones" and "will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them." Representatives of MS NOW declined to comment. What has Trump said about the legality of banning reporters? Trump dismissed concerns about violating the Constitution, telling reporters that the move is justified "because they’re fake news." The president suggested he wanted to make a point, regardless of whether the ban withstands a court challenge. "We'll see," Trump said when asked what makes him think his ban will be upheld in court. "I think it’s good to point it out, whether it survives or doesn’t . . . depends on the judge you get, to be honest with you. I don't think a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day." “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump added. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my , into the people’s house.” Trump had few details on what the ban means in practical terms ‒ whether it's the revocation of press badges, removal from the White House pool, or blocking reporters from the targeted outlets from entering the White House campus. “A very simple ban," Trump said. "I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can.” The president bristled when a reporter asked whether he's trying to intimidate the media from doing its job. "I dislike dishonest press, like you. I think you're terrible. I like to see honest press," the president said. Where does the AP's lawsuit stand? The AP initially had success in its lawsuit challenging the Trump administration's ban. Washington, D.C. federal trial Judge Trevor McFadden, who was appointed by Trump, ruled the ban probably violated the First Amendment's free speech protections and issued a temporary order blocking it. "(U)nder the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists - be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere - it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints," McFadden wrote . However, in a 2-1 decision governed by two other Trump appointees, Judges Neomi Rao and Gregory G. Katsas, an appeals court panel largely struck down McFadden's order. It said blocking the White House from restricting specific reporters' ability to join other reporters in the Oval Office or the press pool interferes with the president's authority. "While the AP has alleged financial loss from being denied access to the Oval Office, that harm does not, inour view, justify an intrusion on presidential prerogatives during this litigation," Rao wrote, in an opinion joined by Katsas. Judge Cornelia T.L. Pillard, an appointee of President Barack Obama, dissented, writing that her colleages' view "cannot be squared with . . . any sensible understanding of the role of a free press in our constitutional democracy." Trump's latest targeted reporter ban appears to go further than the ban on the AP, barring reporters "from the White House," according to his social media post. That may not hold muster even with the judges who largely ruled with the Trump administration before. Those judges did overturn an attempt by the White House to block the AP from accessing the White House's East Room, noting it is "a much larger space that can accommodate more members of the press." And those judges specifically noted the ban on the AP didn't block it from entering White House press facilities such as the main briefing room. The AP's case is still under litigation. What do experts say about the ban? Clay Calvert , a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, called the bans “thoroughly unsurprising,” particularly as Trump faces low approval ratings heading into the midterms. The institute is a Washington-based public policy think tank. The news media is an “easy target” for Trump, Calvert said, and implementing the ban is likely to appeal to his political base that overwhelmingly distrusts mass media . Though it echoes Trump’s earlier ban on the Associated Press, Calvert described that as a “much more precise target” centered on a single decision – the news outlet refusing to adopt “Gulf of America” after Trump renamed the body of water widely known as the “Gulf of Mexico.” The ban was also limited to certain spaces, including Air Force One and the Oval Office. It's not immediately clear whether CNN, MS NOW and Politico would face similar restrictions or be barred from the White House entirely. Barring journalists from the White House or other spaces where the government operates can make it “really difficult” to get information to report to the wider public, ACLU senior policy counsel Jenna Leventoff told USA TODAY. A federal judge blocked a press policy the Pentagon implemented in 2025 that said journalists who "solicit" information not approved for public release could lose access to the building. The Pentagon then imposed an interim press policy that required journalists to be escorted through the premises at all times, which was also struck down . But the potential to get involved in a costly and time-consuming legal fight with the Trump administration may make some news outlets “think twice” about their reporting, Leventoff said. “In that respect, it doesn’t matter if he wins in court or not, because he’s still chilling the media from saying things he dislikes,” she said. National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. said in the organization’s news release on the matter that Trump “weakens one of the nation’s strongest checks on those who hold power” by blocking access to his administration. He said the latest ban would be an “unprecedented assault on press freedom” if implemented and underscored journalists’ role in informing the American public. “A government confident in its actions should never fear independent scrutiny,” he said. Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. Reach BrieAnna at bjfrank@usatoday.com and @brieannafrank on X and Bluesky. item.title: Hundreds of thousands rally in Iran in biggest anti-U.S. display since war began
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
CAIRO (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied Friday in a government-organized show of defiance after months of war, pledging their readiness to take up arms in the biggest such demonstration since the United States and Israel attacked in February. Iran's government has sought to rally the people and stress national unity, even as the economy worsens under a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and new U.S. sanctions. On Friday, it claimed another attack on a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz , a key waterway it has sought to control since the start of the war. Estimates varied of the number of people volunteering to receive limited military training and defend the country in an effort described as "Janfaday-e Iran," or the "ones who sacrifice their lives for Iran." They marched through downtown Tehran in combat uniform, carrying flags, as onlookers cheered. For days, state media have encouraged Iranians to join the campaign, saying training with assault rifles would begin soon. The volunteers would be an additional layer of security to the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and the Basij militia , which has played a key role in quashing anti-government protests . Rally seeks to project strength under US pressure Tehran's Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 people had registered to participate, with over 1 million expected to take part in the training. On Friday morning, the broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people were on the streets. The new head of the Basij, Hossein Taeb , declared in a speech as the rally began that the volunteers will be ready for "full-fledged defense" and similar rallies will take place in other cities soon. The new trainees will make a "nightmare" for Iran's enemies, Taeb added, as President Masoud Pezeshkian, military commanders and other senior officials watched the march. Some participants trampled flags of the U.S. and Israel. Others chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel." "I am here to tell (U.S. President Donald) Trump that we Iranians have no fear about his threats against our homeland," said Marzieh Afaghi, 24, who attended the rally with her toddler and husband. "No one in history could invade Iran and remain there." The rally was also a chance for Iran to show off military hardware. Anti-aircraft batteries were on display, while female Guard members in black headscarves sat with truck-mounted machine guns. Iran says it attacked another tanker in the Strait of Hormuz The Guard displayed drones that have been used against ships in the Strait of Hormuz , where Iran's attacks and threats have severely affected the Gulf region's shipments of oil and natural gas to the rest of the world. Iran said it had attacked a Togo-flagged oil tanker, the Trend, for what it called an "illegal attempt" to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, the state broadcaster reported. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a tanker was hit by a projectile, sparking a fire on board that was extinguished. The UKMTO in a separate update said ship transits facilitated by the U.S. military off Oman have averaged 24 a day over the past week but overall traffic remains about 90% lower than before the war. Iran's new volunteers could help suppress future dissent Friday's events also suggested that hard-liners like Taeb among Iran's leadership will be more prepared to suppress any future demonstration against the theocracy. In January, shortly before the war, Iran saw some of its largest nationwide protests in history, which began over the struggling economy and turned to wider grievances. Activists have said a crackdown killed over 7,000 people and saw tens of thousands detained. In May, government officials said more than 30 million people in Iran — which has a total population of some 90 million — had volunteered via an online form or at public gatherings to lay down their lives for the theocracy. The Associated Press could not independently confirm that. ___ Karimi reported from Tehran, Iran, and Anna from Jerusalem. item.title: Uber must pay $40 million after driver left UCLA grad on freeway, where she was killed
item.description:

Uber has been ordered to pay $40 million to the family of a UCLA graduate who was killed when her driver abandoned her on a freeway. Judge Richard A. Stone ruled that driver Vu Tran “needlessly placed” Emily Normandin-Parker and her friend in danger when he left the pair on State Route 73 in California, according to Panish, Shea, Ravipudi, the law firm representing the family, on Thursday. “Emily did everything Uber tells riders to do—she made the responsible choice not to drive and we trusted Uber to get her home safely. That trust cost our daughter her life,” Emily’s parents Carol Normandin and Ken Parker said. Emily Normandin-Parker was killed in August 2023 after being struck by traffic following a night out. Panish Shea Ravipudi LLP Normandin-Parker, 23, was killed in the early hours of August, 12 2023, following a night out with her pal, Luna Moore, in Costa Mesa. The pair turned to the ride-sharing app, but Moore vomited in driver Tran’s car and he ordered the pair to get out. Normandin-Parker was struck by traffic after Tran parked at a gore point that separated an exit ramp and the California State Route 73 freeway. She was hit by a car while an apoplectic Moore argued with the driver, who wanted a cleaning fee. Normandin and Parker accused Tran and Uber of negligence and were awarded $20 million each following a five-day arbitration hearing in March. Stone, a retired Los Angeles County judge who presided over the hearing, scolded Tran for showing “far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers,” according to court documents seen by The Post. “In a fit of anger, he needlessly placed them (and himself) in danger by illegally stopping in the gore point,” Stone ruled. Tran allegedly racked up complaints from previous passengers over his “reckless” behavior, lawyers argued. His previous riders claimed Tran “cannot drive” and that he was “the least safe” ride that one customer had experienced. Tran tried to claim he wasn’t at fault because Normandin-Parker walked into the traffic – an argument the judge rejected. Uber chiefs tried to keep the award confidential – threatening a $10 million penalty against the parents if they spoke out. “We didn’t have much time to absorb the award before Uber almost immediately started contending that it could not be made public and then sent an agreement to us requiring non-disparagement, the $10 million penalty for saying anything bad about Uber,” Parker told Good Morning America Thursday. item.title: Someone has poisoned 28 Lake Tahoe trees. Now there's a $147,000 reward.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
These three trees, pictured on Aug. 6, are among those recently poisoned at Burnt Cedar Beach in Incline Village, Nev. (Scott Sady / For The Times) A question has bedeviled a wealthy Lake Tahoe enclave for years: Who is poisoning the towering trees that stand sentry on the North Shore? Residents of Incline Village, Nev., hope a $147,000 reward will generate some answers. “It’s the most appalling, selfish thing that anyone could do, especially for trees that are irreplaceable,” said Chris Nolet, a retired certified public accountant and consultant to the biotechnology industry who assembled a small group of private donors known as Friends of Burnt Cedar Beach to put up the bulk of the reward. “These trees are 100 years old.” The donors are offering $122,000 for information leading to the successful prosecution of anyone responsible. The Incline Village General Improvement District, which owns and manages the residents-only beach where the poisonings took place, has put up another $25,000 and installed additional cameras around the trees. The move came after an investigation failed to generate actionable leads, Nolet said. “My feeling is, we’ve got to try something different,” he said, “and money talks.” Read more: A Lake Tahoe murder mystery: Who is poisoning towering pine trees? Someone has, on multiple occasions, slipped into the picturesque wooded cove, drilled holes near the roots of the conifers and poured a chemical inside. A total of 28 trees have been poisoned since 2022 and at least 10 have died, some of them more than a century old. The attacks escalated this summer, with 16 trees — 13 Jeffrey pines and three white firs — poisoned on three occasions between May and early August. It’s too soon to say how many of the trees will survive; some are showing signs of stress including brown needles, according to Sam Gough, an arborist with the Incline Village General Improvement District. “The effects of chemical exposure may develop slowly and may not become fully apparent for several months or even multiple growing seasons,” Gough said Friday at a news conference announcing the reward. Grounds staff have removed contaminated soil from around the affected trees and applied a biochar and compost mixture to support their natural defensive response, she said. They are also hand-watering the trees to reduce environmental stress and give them a better chance of healing, she said. Read more: Mysterious poisoning of Tahoe trees may improve somebody's view Staff will continue regular inspections to detect crown thinning, needle discoloration and loss, reduced growth and abnormal resin production, she said. “It’s a little disheartening to realize that somebody has done something that can’t be repaired — like, this damage cannot be repaired,” Gough said. “In 150 years, new trees could regrow, but we won’t be here for that. It’s a great loss.” Six trees were previously poisoned in 2022, four of which died, according to Paul Raymore, a spokesman for the Incline Village General Improvement District. The next year, six more trees were poisoned and survived. But then in 2024, someone re-poisoned those six trees, and they all died, he said. In the past, diesel fuel was poured around the bases of the trees, and grounds staff said last month that they suspected copper sulfate was dumped into the holes drilled near the roots. The chemical is known to slowly kill trees from the inside out. Read more: Poisoned trees gave a wealthy couple in Maine a killer ocean view. Residents wonder, at what cost? Improvement District representatives said Friday that in the most recent incidents staff observed blue granules inside the holes and smelled a strong odor associated with an unidentified liquid, but they declined to speculate on what chemicals may have been used. Soil samples were provided to the sheriff’s office in Washoe County, Nev., for analysis, they said. The sheriff’s office did not respond to questions about whether it had received the results of that analysis. Read more: A bloody Mojave mystery: Who is target-shooting these beloved ostriches? Although investigators haven’t determined a motive for the arboreal attacks, both residents and law enforcement officers have theorized they may be the work of a homeowner seeking to improve property value . Incline Village has earned the nickname “Income Village” due to its reputation as a haven for Silicon Valley’s ultrawealthy. Lake views are a hot commodity in the community, and buyers pay steep premiums for properties with unobstructed sightlines. Still, because the homes are staggered up a hillside, upward of 100 properties could gain a better lake view from the poisoned trees’ removal, according to the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office. So far, the most compelling piece of evidence publicly reported by authorities was a flash of light captured by a trail camera about 2 a.m. on Aug 2. Authorities are trying to learn how the perpetrator gained access to the beach, including whether they boated over from the other side of the lake, investigators have said. The Tahoe Regional Planning Agency is also investigating the tree poisonings. The agency encourages property owners to remove certain trees around homes for defensible-space purposes and works to thin forests throughout the Tahoe Basin to reduce wildfire risk. But healthy, nonhazardous trees are important to the health of Lake Tahoe and environmental quality in the region, according to spokesman Jeff Cowen. “Root systems protect Lake Tahoe’s clarity by stabilizing soils that could erode, and uptaking nutrients that would feed algae in the lake,” Cowen wrote in an email. “Healthy forests also provide critical wildlife habitat and protect scenic quality.” Nolet has lived in Incline Village for seven years — part-time for 19 — and describes it as one of the most special places on earth, a veritable paradise where residents can boat, ski, fish and bike. “The trees are so innocent and that park is so beautiful,” he said. “It just kind of is beyond the pale to think that people would sneak in there, drill holes in the trunks, fill them full of poison, put the poison around the tree trunks and sneak out.” “That’s an assault on our community that’s not acceptable,” he added. The reward funds will be made available to anyone who provides information by March 31 that results in a successful prosecution within two years of the date it is provided. There’s one caveat: neither the person responsible for the poisonings nor any accessories will be eligible for the money. They could face felony charges, as authorities estimate the trees that were killed or damaged to be worth at least $300,000. Detectives with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office have urged anyone with information, regardless of how insignificant it may seem, to call them at (775) 328-3001 and reference case number 26-4225. Anonymous tips may also be submitted through Secret Witness online or by calling (775) 322-4900. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. item.title: Using food stamps or Medicaid can now put some immigrants' green cards at risk
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Immigrants applying to live permanently in the United States can be rejected if they receive public benefits, beginning this week. Use of Medicaid, food stamps, tuition assistance and free school lunch programs, among other government assistance, could all be grounds for denying a green-card application. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The policy from President Donald Trump’s administration, which took effect Friday, marks a dramatic change to a long-standing federal policy consistent with the president’s efforts to restrict legal immigration pathways. The rule could reduce federal and state payments by $13 billion a year, by persuading some 950,000 people to disenroll from or avoid federal safety net programs, according to estimates from the Department of Homeland Security. The agency said that the rule aligns with Congress’s intent that noncitizens “in the United States be self-sufficient and not dependent on taxpayer-funded government benefits.” “Aliens in the United States should be self-reliant,” a DHS policy document for the rule states, “and government benefits should not incentivize immigration.” Applying for a green card, or legal permanent residency, is a necessary step for those seeking U.S. citizenship. This week, New York led 21 other states, the District of Columbia and several cities in suing the Trump administration over the new rule. The lawsuit argued that the rule fails “to consider many important aspects” of the problems it creates and warned that the harms will extend to mixed-status families and U.S. citizen children. “Cruelty is the point,” New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) said at a news conference announcing the lawsuit this week. “Having a chilling effect on immigrants is the point. Letting individuals know that they are not welcome here is the point.” The rule allows immigration officers to use their judgment in considering whether use of benefits such as food stamps indicates that a person is “likely at any time to become a public charge,” or dependent on government assistance. Critics warn that an absence of clear guidance on which benefits will be considered in a green-card application will led to inconsistent application and a broader chilling effect. “The lack of specificity makes it really hard for any family to know what [government-provided benefit] is safe to use,” said Julia Gelatt, an associate director at the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The Department of Homeland Security rule expands the “public charge” policy in place since 1882. Immigration officers have long factored in a person’s health, finances and skills in determining whether they are likely to rely on government assistance in the future. But only direct cash payments, such as disability income, and long-term hospitalization, previously were considered reasons for denying a green-card application. The new rule applies to immediate family members of U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents, including children and spouses, fiancés of U.S. citizens, skilled and religious workers, and others. Other types of immigrants, including asylum seekers and refugees, will not be subject to the rule. The first Trump administration introduced a similar rule in 2019 that was later blocked by courts. But the policy spread fear and confusion among immigrant households, leading to a sharp drop in people living in households where someone lacked a green card enrolling in noncash federal assistance programs, such as food stamps, according to an Urban Institute report. item.title: Sen. Thom Tillis says 'classic Mitch' has returned
item.description:

WASHINGTON – Senate Republicans' three-month headache about Mitch McConnell's health seems to have subsided – at least for now. In the days since the Kentucky lawmaker's return to the Capitol , they've defended him in the halls and expressed gratitude that his condition has improved. A fall in June, followed by a bout of pneumonia, kept the 84-year-old off the job for much of the summer and complicated the voting math for Senate Republicans on key legislation. On his way back into the Senate chamber on the night of Monday, Sept. 14, he joked with reporters about admittedly dodging their questions since he'd been gone. Sitting in a wheelchair with visibly bruised hands, he resolved that it was "time to get back to work" and "finish the ​job for this Congress." He isn't running for reelection and will end his more than 40-year Senate tenure by January. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, who's served in the Senate with McConnell for more than a decade and will also retire next year, said he had a "great conversation" with him on Thursday. It was "classic Mitch," Tillis told USA TODAY. "I spent 20 seconds asking him how he's doing, and he goes right into preserving the filibuster, and who we have to look ahead to do it as we leave, and Ukraine," Tillis said. McConnell has been a vocal proponent of maintaining U.S. military and diplomatic support for Ukraine amid its ongoing war with Russia, as well as shielding the filibuster, the 60-vote threshold in the Senate that he says encourages bipartisanship, from President Donald Trump 's campaign to eliminate it. Congress' age conundrum: At 93, Sen. Chuck Grassley still doing the job His reemergence in the Capitol took the internet by storm. One moment in particular stood out : During a meeting of the Senate Agriculture Committee to vote on the farm bill, it appeared to some onlookers as though McConnell voted incorrectly, raising more questions about his mental state. When McConnell voted yes, Sen. John Hoeven, R-North Dakota, leaned over and said something to him. But Hoeven told USA TODAY he wasn't correcting McConnell – he himself wasn't sure about whether they were taking a more procedural vote or voting on final passage of the bill out of committee. "He voted, and he voted correctly," Hoeven said. "He was there. He was present. He got it right." Hoeven and other Senate Republicans said they were happy to have McConnell back. The Senate will be in session for another two weeks before going on recess for more than a month until after the midterm elections in November. "I haven't had a chance to run into him," Rand Paul, McConnell's Kentucky counterpart in the Senate, told USA TODAY. "But I'm glad he's back and glad he's doing better." item.title: 'Resident Evil' review: Zach Cregger's video game adaptation is easily the best 'Resident Evil' movie yet
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Austin Abrams in Zach Cregger's Resident Evil . Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photo: Sony Pictures Releasing/Everett Collection Ahead of the release of Zach Cregger's reboot today, there were already seven Resident Evil movies — six of them in a more action-oriented series starring Milla Jovovich, four of which were directed by her husband, Paul W.S. Anderson, plus an unrelated "reboot" in 2021 called Welcome to Raccoon City that went for more of a John Carpenter vibe and was an attempt to truly "adapt" the games. There's also a Netflix TV show version that ran for a single season in 2022. Countless other works in the horror genre have unofficially cribbed from the Resident Evil games over the years. It's an incredibly influential series. And yet, Zach Cregger, hot off his Oscar-winning original horror film Weapons, is the first filmmaker to truly feel like he's adapting the experience of playing the games, arguably the scariest survival-horror ones ever made, rather than simply incorporating story and plot elements to explain the outbreak of infected people. In Cregger's hands, Resident Evil is pure crowd-pleasing popcorn cinema, best experienced in a packed movie theater with dozens of other people reacting loudly to the madness. The premise couldn't be simpler — and the runtime a brisk 90ish minutes — as we follow a medical courier named Bryan (Austin Abrams, proving himself to be the Bruce Campbell for a new generation) who unwittingly finds himself fighting for survival as one fateful, horrifying night collapses around him in a swirl of chaos. Fans of the video games will recognize various easter eggs and nods to game mechanics, including the importance of conserving ammo and checking every last drawer for more of it. But you don't need to be familiar with the games at all to enjoy the movie, which is an efficient horror set-piece machine that just keeps putting Abrams in increasingly concerning situations. I can't stress enough how much this is a one-man show anchored by Abrams, and he crushes it. He's in every scene, earning tons of laughs simply by reacting as a normal person would in this situation; he's a true audience-surrogate character, ushering us through the chaos. His comedic timing, paired with Cregger's assured camerawork and editing, is a match made in genre-movie heaven. I didn't expect it to be so heavily inspired by genre classics like The Thing and Evil Dead. In fact, it's a better Evil Dead movie than the last several movies with " Evil Dead " in the title, nailing the horror-comedy tone that only Sam Raimi and a few others can pull off with aplomb. Cregger has a ton of fun with the various monstrous forms that the infected take here, from fusing multiple humans together to crafting his own horror take on a big, scary guy like Dune 's Baron Harkonnen. Resident Evil movies have thus far treated the zombies as pretty traditional movie zombies; Cregger's version gets at the attempt to create the next stage of human evolution. Zach Cregger's Resident Evil may not feature characters that gaming fans recognize, but it's spiritually more in line with the games than any of the ones that do. Adaptation stuff aside, it's also just a heart-pounding, adrenaline-fueled roller coaster ride of a movie that has no grander ambitions than getting a rise out of the audience over and over again. It's a blast, and this time, you can't pause it, put your controller down, and walk away when things get too intense.
